summary.text: White blood cells, or leukocytes, are cells of the immune system that protect the body against infectious disease and foreign entities.
They include three main subtypes, granulocytes, lymphocytes, and monocytes, and all are made from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.
Unlike red blood cells and platelets they have nuclei, and they make up about 1% of the blood volume of a healthy adult.

facts.label: Normal count
facts.value: 4,000 to 11,000 per microliter in the US

facts.label: Share of blood
facts.value: About 1% of volume in a healthy adult

facts.label: Where they are made
facts.value: Bone marrow, from hematopoietic stem cells

facts.label: Low count
facts.value: Called leukopenia, indicating a weakened immune system

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: A pale layer in a centrifuged blood sample

items.prompt: Under a microscope, what feature sets white blood cells apart from red blood cells and platelets?

options.label: They have nuclei
They are always smaller than platelets
They are found only outside the blood
They are made in the liver

items.explain: All white blood cells have nuclei, unlike the anucleated red blood cells and platelets.

items.prompt: A person with a bad cold has a white cell count well above 11,000 per microliter. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Red blood cells have crowded the white cells out
The bone marrow has stopped producing cells
The body is responding to infection or inflammation
The immune system has become weaker

items.explain: An excess of white blood cells is usually due to infection or inflammation.

items.prompt: A person's white blood cell count falls below the normal lower limit. What does that suggest?

options.label: A weakened immune system
An unusually strong immune system
Too many red blood cells
A healthy response to infection

items.explain: A count below the lower limit is called leukopenia, which indicates a weakened immune system.

items.prompt: Where do all white blood cells ultimately come from?

options.label: Hepatocytes in the liver
Platelets in the blood
Red blood cells in the spleen
Stem cells in the bone marrow

items.explain: All white blood cells derive from multipotent hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.

items.prompt: Blood looks red, so why are these cells called 'white'?

options.label: They carry a white pigment inside
They form a thin whitish layer when a blood sample is spun
They turn white after meeting a germ
They are bleached by oxygen in the lungs

items.explain: After centrifugation, white cells sit in the buffy coat, a thin, typically white layer between the red cells and the plasma.

items.prompt: T cells and B cells belong to which of the two big lineage families of white blood cells?

options.label: Myeloid cells
Mast cells
Lymphoid cells
Granulocytes

items.explain: White blood cells are classified by lineage as myeloid or lymphoid, and lymphocytes such as T and B cells are lymphoid.

paragraphs.heading: The body's defenders
paragraphs.text: White blood cells, also called leukocytes or immune cells, are the cells of the immune system. Their job is to guard the body against infectious disease and against foreign things that get inside. They help it fight off infection and other illnesses. They travel all over the body, in the blood and in the lymphatic system.

paragraphs.heading: How they differ from other blood cells
paragraphs.text: White blood cells are generally bigger than red blood cells. Each one has a nucleus, and that sets them apart from red blood cells and platelets, which have none. Every type is made in the bone marrow from multipotent cells there called hematopoietic stem cells.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The name comes from what blood looks like after it is spun in a centrifuge. The white cells settle in the buffy coat, a thin layer, usually white, that sits between the packed red cells and the plasma. The scientific name says the same thing: leuk- is Greek for white and cyt- for cell. If a sample holds many neutrophils, the buffy coat can look green, from an enzyme called myeloperoxidase that they make.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting the types
paragraphs.text: There are two broad ways to group them. One looks at structure: granulocytes have a lobed nucleus and visible grains in their cytoplasm, while agranulocytes have a round nucleus and no visible grains. The other looks at lineage, the line of development a cell comes from: myeloid cells versus lymphoid cells, or lymphocytes. Together these give five main types: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes and monocytes.

paragraphs.heading: Eaters and specialists
paragraphs.text: Monocytes, macrophages and neutrophils are all phagocytic cells. Neutrophils are the most common kind, making up 60 to 70% of the white cells in circulation, and they fight bacterial and fungal infections. Lymphocytes split further into T cells, B cells and natural killer cells. Monocytes are further divided into dendritic cells and macrophages.

paragraphs.heading: Small numbers, large effect
paragraphs.text: In a healthy adult, white cells are only about 1% of the blood's volume, far fewer than red cells at 40 to 45%. Yet immunity depends on that 1%. A normal count is usually 4,000 to 11,000 cells per microlitre of blood. A count above the upper limit is called leukocytosis, and it is normal when it comes from a healthy immune response, while a count below the lower limit, called leukopenia, points to a weakened immune system.
